questions.question: What is the primary role of the self-attention mechanism within a transformer layer?
questions.choice_A: To let each token weight and aggregate information from all other tokens in the sequence based on learned relevance
questions.choice_B: To compress the sequence into a fixed-length vector before classification
questions.choice_C: To enforce a strict left-to-right dependency without any context mixing
questions.choice_D: To reduce parameter count by sharing weights across all layers

questions.question: Why are multiple heads used in multi-head attention?
questions.choice_A: To independently compute positional encodings at different frequencies
questions.choice_B: To enable the model to attend to different types of relations or subspaces in parallel
questions.choice_C: To reduce the quadratic complexity of attention to linear complexity
questions.choice_D: To ensure numerical stability during layer normalization

questions.question: In transformer encoders versus decoders, which architectural distinction is most central?
questions.choice_A: Encoders use only feedforward layers while decoders use only attention layers
questions.choice_B: Encoders have masked self-attention while decoders use unmasked self-attention
questions.choice_C: Encoders use bidirectional self-attention, while decoders use causal (masked) self-attention
questions.choice_D: Encoders share parameters across layers, while decoders do not

questions.question: What is the function of positional encodings in transformers?
questions.choice_A: They regularize training by randomly dropping tokens
questions.choice_B: They provide token identities to the model to replace embeddings
questions.choice_C: They inject information about sequence order into an otherwise permutation-invariant architecture
questions.choice_D: They lower the computational complexity of attention from $O(n^2)$ to $O(n)$

questions.question: Why are residual connections used around sublayers (attention and feedforward) in transformers?
questions.choice_A: They facilitate gradient flow and stabilize training by allowing identity mapping paths
questions.choice_B: They reduce the number of parameters by reusing earlier activations
questions.choice_C: They enforce sparsity in attention weights during pretraining
questions.choice_D: They replace the need for layer normalization altogether

questions.question: In a standard transformer block, what is the typical order of operations when using Pre-LN (pre–layer normalization) architecture?
questions.choice_A: Self-attention, residual add, feedforward, residual add, layer normalization
questions.choice_B: Layer normalization, self-attention, residual add; layer normalization, feedforward, residual add
questions.choice_C: Feedforward, layer normalization, residual add; self-attention, layer normalization, residual add
questions.choice_D: Residual add, layer normalization, self-attention; residual add, layer normalization, feedforward

questions.question: What objective is optimized in causal language modeling (CLM) pretraining?
questions.choice_A: Predicting the next token given only the final hidden state
questions.choice_B: Predicting masked tokens anywhere in the input using full bidirectional context
questions.choice_C: Predicting the next token given all previous tokens using a causal mask
questions.choice_D: Predicting sentence order for a pair of sentences

questions.question: Which of the following best describes masked language modeling (MLM) as in BERT?
questions.choice_A: Predict the next token auto-regressively with no masking
questions.choice_B: Randomly mask a subset of tokens and train the model to reconstruct them using both left and right context
questions.choice_C: Generate an entire sequence from noise using a diffusion process
questions.choice_D: Predict whether two sentences are paraphrases without token-level supervision

questions.question: Why do large-scale, diverse pretraining datasets often improve downstream transfer?
questions.choice_A: They reduce the need for positional encodings by making the model robust to order
questions.choice_B: They expose the model to varied patterns and tasks, enabling broad representations that can be adapted with limited task-specific data
questions.choice_C: They guarantee lower inference latency due to better tokenization
questions.choice_D: They allow exact memorization of all downstream datasets encountered later

questions.question: Which statement about multi-head attention parameterization is accurate?
questions.choice_A: Each head uses its own projection matrices for queries, keys, and values before concatenation
questions.choice_B: All heads share a single projection matrix to prevent overfitting
questions.choice_C: Heads compute attention in disjoint token spans to enforce locality
questions.choice_D: Heads always attend to identical patterns because they are constrained to be orthogonal

questions.question: How do scaling laws inform the design of pretraining runs?
questions.choice_A: They show that deeper models always outperform wider ones at the same parameter count
questions.choice_B: They provide empirical power-law relationships between loss, model size, data size, and compute, guiding compute-optimal trade-offs
questions.choice_C: They prove that model performance saturates after a fixed number of tokens, independent of size
questions.choice_D: They dictate that learning rate should scale linearly with the square root of parameters

questions.question: What is a primary difference between instruction tuning and standard fine-tuning?
questions.choice_A: Instruction tuning trains only the embedding layer, while fine-tuning trains all layers
questions.choice_B: Instruction tuning uses curated examples of tasks framed as instructions and responses to align behavior, not just optimize task loss
questions.choice_C: Instruction tuning requires no labeled data, while fine-tuning does
questions.choice_D: Instruction tuning is performed only on encoders, while fine-tuning is for decoders

questions.question: Why is layer normalization important in transformer training?
questions.choice_A: It enforces sparsity in attention maps, improving interpretability
questions.choice_B: It stabilizes activations and gradients across tokens and features, enabling deeper and more stable training
questions.choice_C: It reduces the need for residual connections by normalizing outputs to zero
questions.choice_D: It replaces the softmax in attention to avoid overflow

questions.question: What practical technique helps fit longer sequences into GPU memory during pretraining?
questions.choice_A: Replacing self-attention with recurrent layers
questions.choice_B: Gradient checkpointing to trade compute for memory by recomputing activations in the backward pass
questions.choice_C: Removing positional encodings to shorten sequence representations
questions.choice_D: Using larger batch sizes to amortize memory across devices

questions.question: Which challenge arises from the quadratic complexity of self-attention with respect to sequence length $n$?
questions.choice_A: Model capacity becomes independent of parameter count
questions.choice_B: Training becomes unstable due to vanishing gradients
questions.choice_C: Memory and compute scale as $O(n^2)$, making very long context windows expensive
questions.choice_D: Token embeddings cannot be shared across vocabulary items

questions.question: What is the role of the position-wise feedforward network (FFN) in a transformer block?
questions.choice_A: It computes attention weights between token pairs
questions.choice_B: It performs the final classification over labels
questions.choice_C: It applies a non-linear transformation independently to each token's representation to increase model expressivity
questions.choice_D: It aggregates token representations by averaging

questions.question: How does causal masking differ from bidirectional attention masking?
questions.choice_A: Causal masking hides future tokens from each position, while bidirectional masking allows each position to see both left and right context
questions.choice_B: Causal masking hides both past and future tokens, while bidirectional masking hides none
questions.choice_C: Causal masking is used only in encoders, while bidirectional masking is used only in decoders
questions.choice_D: They are identical; both allow full-context attention

questions.question: What is a common strategy to increase effective batch size without increasing per-device memory usage?
questions.choice_A: Using smaller models at inference
questions.choice_B: Accumulating gradients over multiple micro-batches before an optimizer step
questions.choice_C: Disabling residual connections to free memory
questions.choice_D: Switching to character-level tokenization

questions.question: During autoregressive inference with long sequences, what optimization reduces compute for subsequent tokens?
questions.choice_A: Recomputing all attention scores from scratch at every step
questions.choice_B: Caching keys and values from previous time steps (KV caching)
questions.choice_C: Replacing softmax with linear activation
questions.choice_D: Using bidirectional masking at inference time

questions.question: Why can instruction-tuned models generalize better to new task formats than purely task-finetuned models?
questions.choice_A: They are trained with explicit objectives to minimize perplexity on general text
questions.choice_B: They learn to map diverse natural language instructions to appropriate behaviors, improving robustness to formatting and task descriptions
questions.choice_C: They use fewer parameters and therefore avoid overfitting
questions.choice_D: They exclude any domain-specific data during training
